body_markdown:
What to confirm before leaving a PEO
Before you leave a PEO, a co-employment arrangement, put in writing which entity reported your wages under which employer identification number (EIN), which pay dates fall before and after the end date, who will administer health coverage and retirement plans, and how you will receive your payroll records. If your PEO was a certified professional employer organization (CPEO), federal rules add a Form 8973 filing and, for worksite employees, a wage-base handoff in the year you switch.
How to confirm what changes on payroll when the PEO contract ends
The IRS describes the CPEO program as a voluntary certification of PEOs, and a PEO is a CPEO from the effective date of its certification until the IRS revokes that certification or the CPEO voluntarily terminates it. A CPEO files aggregate employment tax returns under its own EIN and allocates each customer’s wages on Schedule R by the customer’s EIN. The IRS calls the business that signs a CPEO contract the customer, and the CPEO rules in this guide apply only if your PEO was a CPEO, and the wage-base handoff and the credit rules also require that the employee was a worksite employee, a covered employee at a work site where at least 85 percent of the individuals performing services for the customer are covered by CPEO contracts.


What you need first. Your PEO agreement and schedules, the PEO’s exact legal name and EIN as written, and your own EIN.


1. Check the entity name against the IRS list of certified CPEOs, which is updated quarterly, and the IRS lists of suspended and revoked CPEOs. One brand name can cover more than one entity, and a CPEO contract must show the CPEO’s exact name and EIN.
2. Ask for the Form 8973 copy. At contract start the CPEO must give the customer a copy of the completed, signed Form 8973, and if a customer does not sign it, section 3511 does not apply to that customer.
3. Read line 5 of Form 8973, which names the returns the CPEO reports (Forms 940, 941, 943 and CT-1) and says whether it reports all or some wages.


What a correct result looks like. You can say which entity reported your wages under which EIN for each quarter of the contract. If your PEO was not a CPEO, you hold its written answer to the same question instead.
How to sort the filings that split in the year you switch
Form W-2 entries must be based on wages paid during the calendar year, so the pay date, not the work period or the contract end date alone, decides which filer reports a wage.


What you need first. The contract end date, your pay calendar with quarter ends marked, and year-to-date wages by employee.


1. List the last pay date the PEO paid and the first pay date you paid yourself, then map every wage paid to the filer that paid it. When an employer and a CPEO or other third-party payer both paid an employee in a quarter, each files Form 941 for the wages it paid, and each issues Forms W-2 for the wages it paid.
2. Note the wage-base handoff, which applies only to a worksite employee of a CPEO. When the contract ends, the customer is treated as a successor employer and the CPEO as the predecessor for the FICA and FUTA annual wage limits, under section 3511 and the Treasury regulation. The regulation applies that treatment to the annual wage limitations and the railroad retirement contribution base, and keeps the Additional Medicare Tax withholding threshold separate for pay from a CPEO.
3. Check year-to-date wages against the limits. As of October 2026, the 2026 Social Security tax rate is 6.2 percent each for employer and employee on wages up to $184,500, the Social Security Administration lists $192,300 for 2027, and FUTA applies to the first $7,000 paid to each employee. Each limit applies per employee per calendar year, so it resets each January 1.
4. Ask the date the end Form 8973 will be filed (question 2). A CPEO files Form 8973 within 30 days of starting or ending a service contract, and the customer may separately file its own Form 8973 to report the end, though that is not required.


Hypothetical example. Assume a worksite employee is paid $20,000 per month in 2026. The CPEO pays January to June, $120,000, and the contract ends June 30, so the CPEO files Form 8973 for the end by July 30. The customer pays July to December, $120,000, under its own EIN. The CPEO’s employer share of Social Security tax is $120,000 x 6.2 percent = $7,440.00. Because the customer is the successor employer, its Social Security wages for this employee are $184,500 minus $120,000 = $64,500, and its employer share is $64,500 x 6.2 percent = $3,999.00. Together the shares equal $11,439.00, which is 6.2 percent of $184,500. Without the handoff the customer would report $120,000, an employer share of $7,440.00, or $3,441.00 more. The example leaves out FUTA, state taxes and other tax detail.


What a correct result looks like. Every wage paid appears on one filer’s returns, and each employee paid by both you and the former PEO has a Form W-2 from each for the wages that filer paid.
How to set up payroll under your own EIN before the first pay date
What you need first. Your IRS EIN notices and any IRS account access details.


1. Enroll in EFTPS or set up your business tax account, where eligible businesses can view tax transcripts. Federal tax deposits must be made by electronic funds transfer, which can use EFTPS, IRS Direct Pay or the business tax account, and EFTPS enrollment can take up to five business days.
2. Put your first Form 941 on the calendar. A business files its first Form 941 for the quarter in which it first pays wages, then every quarter, even with no tax to report, unless it has filed a final return or an exception applies.
3. Check your address of record and responsible party. The IRS strongly recommends that an employer keep its own address as its IRS address of record, because IRS correspondence goes there. Form 8822-B reports a changed business address, location or responsible party, and a responsible-party change is due within 60 days (question 17).
4. Ask the IRS or a tax adviser which deposit schedule applies to you, because a Form 941 filer’s schedule is determined from the taxes reported in a four-quarter lookback period.


What a correct result looks like. You can sign in to EFTPS or your business tax account under your own EIN, your first Form 941 quarter is on the calendar, and the IRS or a tax adviser has confirmed which deposit schedule applies to you.


Employers that plan to run payroll and HR themselves after leaving can look at AsureCentral, a unified payroll and HR platform with one login for growing employers that manage payroll and HR internally.
How to confirm health coverage and retirement plan terms
What you need first. Your health plan documents, renewal dates, current COBRA participant list and retirement plan type.


1. Ask for the coverage end date of each health plan and for claims run-out, accumulator and flexible spending documentation (questions 12 and 13).
2. Ask who administers COBRA (question 12).
3. Note employee options. People who lose group health coverage may have a 30-day special enrollment period to join another group health plan, and HealthCare.gov says a loss of employer coverage may qualify a person for a Marketplace Special Enrollment Period within 60 days before or after the loss.
4. Ask for the retirement plan type and read the exit terms in the plan documents (question 15). The IRS defines a multiple employer plan as one maintained by two or more employers who are not related and says to review the plan document for testing and correction provisions.
5. If your business is an applicable large employer under the Affordable Care Act, ask who files Forms 1094-C and 1095-C for each month of the switch year (question 14).


What a correct result looks like. You hold written coverage end dates, a named COBRA administrator and the exit terms from your plan documents.
How to confirm unemployment insurance and workers’ compensation accounts
What you need first. Your state unemployment account numbers and your workers’ compensation policy details.


1. Ask the former PEO about your state accounts (question 11).
2. Contact each state agency. State law determines state unemployment insurance tax rates, and employers should contact their state workforce agencies, and the DOL lists state contacts. For a private-employer workplace injury, the DOL points people to the state workers’ compensation board.


What a correct result looks like. Each state account has a named owner and a start date for your business.
How to leave with the records you need
What you need first. A list of the records the PEO ran and a retention calendar.


1. Request payroll registers, Forms W-4, deposit records and copies of returns for every pay period the PEO ran.
2. Ask which years the Form 8973 consent covers (question 9). The form includes a CPEO consent that lets the IRS disclose to the customer information from the CPEO’s returns about that customer, for the years listed.
3. Ask what credit information you will receive (question 10). For research, work opportunity and similar credits, the customer, not the CPEO, takes the wages and taxes into account, and the CPEO must give the customer the information to claim them.
4. Set retention dates. Employers must keep employment tax records for at least 4 years. The IRS says to keep Form W-2 Copy A and Form W-3 for at least 4 years, and the DOL says FLSA payroll records must be kept at least three years. A CPEO contract must say the CPEO will keep employee records for covered individuals (question 8).


What a correct result looks like. You hold records for every PEO-run pay period in a format you can open and search, and each retention date is on your calendar.
How to put your questions in writing before you give notice
What you need first. The contract’s notice terms and your lists of employees, plans and state accounts.


1. Send the questions below to the former PEO as one written request. Put questions about your new setup, such as under whose EIN it will file Forms 941, 940, W-2 and W-3, to your new provider.
2. Check the right-hand column to see which questions are tied to a federal rule, plan documents, a state agency or IRS records, and which are contract matters or items to confirm in writing.
3. Keep every reply with your payroll records.


What a correct result looks like. Each answer is dated and in writing, and contract matters are checked against the contract itself.

Frequently asked questions
Will an employee get two Forms W-2 in the year we leave?
If the former PEO paid an employee under its own EIN and your business paid the same employee under yours later in the year, each of you issues a Form W-2 for the wages it paid. The EIN on a Form W-2 must be the one used on that employer’s federal employment tax returns.
Does the Social Security wage base restart when we leave?
Not during the same calendar year if the PEO was a CPEO, section 3511 applied to your contract and the employee was a worksite employee, because the IRS rules treat you as the successor employer and count the wages the CPEO paid that year toward the base. For any other PEO arrangement, ask a tax adviser.
Who handles COBRA after we leave?
Ask the PEO in writing who administers COBRA for current participants and who sends the notices (question 12). The DOL says each plan subject to COBRA must have a designated plan administrator who gives the required notices.
Can we see what the PEO deposited for us?
If your PEO was a CPEO, the IRS says a customer cannot view the federal tax deposits and payments the CPEO made in EFTPS. For any other PEO arrangement, ask which returns it filed (question 3).
